text:
Help me write an open letter. I own an independent pharmacy, and I'm writing for 38 independent pharmacies in our state to the state employees' health plan. We'll send it to the plan and to the two newspapers in the capital.

Facts:
- Since January the plan pays us on average $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and fill it, for the 20 generic drugs we fill most.
- Plan members make up about 22% of the prescriptions at our 38 pharmacies.
- 9 independent pharmacies in the state closed in the last 2 years. We don't know how many closed because of rates.
- In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one.
- The plan's contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1.
- My own pharmacy filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members last year.

I want the letter to say that a third of the independent pharmacies in the state will close within a year if nothing changes. One page.

Before I draft, a few questions. The answers will change what the letter can say.

1. **What is the "a third will close within a year" figure based on?** The facts you gave don't support it yet. Nine closures in two years is about 4–5 a year, and you don't know how many were caused by rates. Do you have a survey of members, owners' own estimates, or financial data showing how long pharmacies can absorb the loss? If you do, I'll cite it. If you don't, the plan's PBM will point that out publicly, and reporters will too. In that case I'd say something you can defend, like "X of our 38 pharmacies tell us they cannot sustain these rates past [date]," or I'd let the per-prescription loss make the case on its own.

2. **What exactly do you want the plan to do?** For example, require a reimbursement floor (cost plus a dispensing fee) in the July 1 PBM contract, require pass-through pricing, or meet with you before renewal. One concrete ask by a set date will work better than a general plea.

3. **Names:** the state, the plan, the PBM (if you're willing to name it publicly), and how the letter is signed. Is it all 38 pharmacies listed by name and town, you on behalf of a group, or an association?

4. **How many independent pharmacies are there in the state in total?** And can you name a few of the 14 counties where an independent is the nearest pharmacy? Specific places make it real to readers and to legislators in those districts.

5. **Is there one patient story you can use** with permission or anonymized? For example, a state employee or retiree in one of those counties who would have to drive a long way if the local pharmacy closed. Also, do you want your 3,100 prescriptions turned into a dollar figure? At $1.80 that's about $5,580 a year, but only if all of those were among the 20 generics, so tell me whether they were.

1. Fair point, I don't have anything behind the "a third" number. Use something the facts support instead. What I do know: two of our 38 pharmacies have told me they'll stop filling for plan members if nothing changes. Some of us make up part of the loss on brand-name drugs, but I don't know by how much.

2. We want the July 1 renewal to pay at least what the drug costs us, plus a fill fee. I can commit to sharing our purchase invoices for the 20 drugs with the plan, and to meeting with the plan's staff any time before May 1.

3. The group is the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance. Sign it from me, Tom Reilly, owner of Reilly Drug in Carver, on behalf of the Alliance. I don't know about naming the state, the plan, or the PBM yet.

4. I don't know the total number of independents in the state. I don't have the county names in front of me. In those 14 counties the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away for most people.

5. I don't have a patient story. I don't know if all 3,100 were among the 20 generics, so I wouldn't use the $5,580 figure as is.

<final_document>
**An Open Letter to the [State Employees' Health Plan]**

[Date]

To [name and title] and the [Plan] board:

We are 38 independent pharmacies in [State], and together we make up the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance. About one in five prescriptions we fill is for a state employee, retiree or family member covered by your plan. We are writing because since January your plan has paid us less than it costs us to fill many of those prescriptions. Some of our pharmacies cannot keep doing that.

**What the rates do**

Your plan sets our pay through its pharmacy benefit manager, [PBM]. For the 20 generic drugs we fill most often, it pays us an average of $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and dispense the drug. Some of us recover part of that loss on brand-name drugs. But a pharmacy can't stay open if it loses money on the medicines it fills most often.

Two of our 38 pharmacies have told us they will stop filling prescriptions for plan members if the rates don't change. Nine independent pharmacies in [State] have closed in the past two years. We don't know how many of those closed because of rates, and we won't claim to. We do know that rates below cost make more closures likely.

**Who it affects**

In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most residents is an independent one. For most people there, the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away. If the local pharmacy in one of those counties stops taking your plan, the state workers and retirees who live there will have to drive that distance or wait for mail order to get their medicine.

**What we ask**

Your contract with [PBM] comes up for renewal on July 1. We ask that the new contract pay pharmacies at least what each drug costs them, plus a dispensing fee for the work of filling it.

We will help you check our numbers:

- We will share our purchase invoices for these 20 drugs with your staff, so you can compare what we pay with what you pay us.
- We will meet with your staff at any time before May 1.

Last year my own pharmacy, Reilly Drug in Carver, filled about 3,100 prescriptions for your members. I want to keep filling them, and so do the other 37 pharmacies in the Alliance. Before you sign the next contract, please let us show you our costs.

Sincerely,

Tom Reilly
Owner, Reilly Drug, Carver
On behalf of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance
[phone / email]
</final_document>

Before you send it, a few things to check:

- **Brackets:** Fill in or remove the state, plan, PBM, addressee, date and contact details. If you decide not to name the PBM, the second section can say "through its pharmacy benefit manager" with no name. Without at least the plan and the state, though, the newspapers probably won't run it, so that's worth deciding.
- **Left out on purpose:** There's no closure forecast and no dollar figure for your 3,100 prescriptions. Everything in the letter comes from the facts you gave me, so the plan can't easily dispute any of it.
- **Easy to strengthen later:** You can add the county names, the dollar amount of the fill fee you want, or the number of pharmacies willing to sign by name. All three would make it harder for the plan to ignore. The letter works without them.
